transcript.answer:
Short answer
- Root cause: ledger-api v1.4.2 processes hit EMFILE ("Too many open files") and started failing accept() calls. That made the /healthz readiness endpoint return errors (connection refused → HTTP 503), so kubelet marked those pods NotReady.
- Affected pods (3 of 6): ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4, ledger-api-866db84748-cz4wp, ledger-api-866db84748-vv6jk — all running on node rcabench-worker2 and showing Ready=0/1. The other three replicas on rcabench-worker are Ready.

What I observed (evidence & timeline)
- Deployment update to APP_VERSION=1.4.2 (image: python:3.12-alpine). Deployment created/rolled at 2026-10-07T09:43:20Z; new pods started ~2026-10-07T09:44:11–12Z.
- Application logs from failing pods (examples):
  2026-10-07T09:45:33Z ERROR ledger-api accept failed: [Errno 24] Too many open files
  (repeated every ~10s thereafter)
- Kubelet events/readiness:
  - Initial readiness failures were "connection refused" immediately after start.
  - Later readiness probe failures show HTTP 503 (kubelet logged HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503).
- Current cluster state:
  - Deployment shows updatedReplicas: 6, availableReplicas: 3, unavailableReplicas: 3.
  - The three NotReady pods are all on node rcabench-worker2; node rcabench-worker remains Ready and hosts the three Ready pods.

Why this is the root cause (five-whys summary)
1. Why are pods NotReady? Their readiness probe fails (ContainersReady = False).
2. Why do readiness probes fail? The app either refused connections or returned 503 for /healthz.
3. Why did the app refuse/return 503? The process was failing accept() with "[Errno 24] Too many open files".
4. Why "[Errno 24]"? The process exhausted its file-descriptor limit (either because the new version leaks FDs or because the process/node ulimits are too low for the runtime behavior).
5. Why only half the pods? All pods run the same image, but the three failing pods are colocated on rcabench-worker2. Possible explanations:
   - the node rcabench-worker2 has lower host/container file-descriptor limits or different runtime ulimits;
   - or that node experienced heavier connection/traffic load so its replicas hit the FD ceiling first;
   - or the new code in 1.4.2 exhibits a file-descriptor leak that manifests quickly when multiple instances land on the same node.

Immediate mitigations (pick one, in order)
1. Roll back the rollout to the previous version (safe, fast):
   - kubectl rollout undo deployment/ledger-api -n ledger
   - kubectl rollout status deployment/ledger-api -n ledger
   This removes the version exposing the leak and will restore availability while you investigate/fix 1.4.2.
2. If rollback is not acceptable: restart the affected node / pods to clear FD exhaustion (short-term only):
   - kubectl delete pod ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 ledger-api-866db84748-cz4wp ledger-api-866db84748-vv6jk -n ledger
   - or cordon & reboot rcabench-worker2 (node restart clears host-level state).
   Note: restarts may only temporarily help if the release has a leak — pods will re-deplete FDs.
3. Reduce incoming load to instances on rcabench-worker2 (if possible) while you diagnose (e.g., temporarily scale down, change service routing).

Recommended diagnostics to run now (to confirm and narrow the cause)
- From a failing pod (or during a live incident, run as appropriate):
  - Count open fds for main process:
    kubectl exec -n ledger -it <pod> -- sh -c "ls -l /proc/1/fd | wc -l"
  - Check process limits:
    kubectl exec -n ledger -it <pod> -- cat /proc/1/limits | grep -i "open files"
  - List types of fds (sockets/files):
    kubectl exec -n ledger -it <pod> -- sh -c "ls -l /proc/1/fd | sed -n '1,200p'"
  - If lsof is available in the image:
    kubectl exec -n ledger -it <pod> -- lsof -p 1 | head -50
- Check host/node limits and usage on rcabench-worker2:
  - ssh to node or run privileged debug pod and check:
    cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max
    sysctl fs.file-max
    ps aux | grep ledger_api (to inspect other processes)
  - Check container runtime/global ulimit settings (how the CRI launches containers).
- Compare the same checks on rcabench-worker (where pods are healthy) to see node differences.

Longer-term fixes
- If code leak: fix the 1.4.2 code to close sockets/FDs and add unit tests to prevent regression. Release a patched 1.4.3.
- Add FD usage monitoring/alerting (process open-fd metric per pod). Grafana/Prometheus: process_open_fds.
- Add a liveness probe that restarts the pod if FD exhaustion causes unhealthy but not crash (careful — this is a mitigation, not a fix).
- Consider increasing node/container open-file limits if application legitimately needs more concurrent sockets:
  - Raise host ulimits (systemd/container runtime configuration) and/or adjust CRI settings that set container ulimits.
  - Ensure resource limits/requests are set and use horizontal autoscaling instead of packing many replicas on one node.
- Harden rollout strategy: smaller maxSurge, health-check based pause, canary to catch regressions earlier.

Commands I used to reach these conclusions (so you can reproduce)
- kubectl get pods -n ledger -o wide
- kubectl describe pod <failing-pod> -n ledger
- kubectl logs <failing-pod> -n ledger --since=30m
- kubectl get deploy ledger-api -n ledger -o yaml
- kubectl describe node rcabench-worker2
- kubectl get events -n ledger --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'

Closing recommendation (short)
- Immediately rollback to the previous release (kubectl rollout undo ...) to restore full availability.
- While rollback is in progress, collect the FD counts and limits from one failing pod and from rcabench-worker2 and compare to rcabench-worker. That will quickly confirm whether this is a per-process leak or a node/ulimit configuration difference. If you want, I can provide the exact commands to run on a failing pod and on the node, or I can attempt further live checks if you give permission to exec into pods or to run a debug pod.
